summary: A quiet weekend after a busy week: youth unemployment climbs to 13.7%, the budget debate rolls on, and elementary teachers start strike votes today.
body: It was a quiet weekend, so the most useful news is still Friday's jobs report. Canada lost 4,700 jobs in October and unemployment rose to 6.7%, Statistics Canada says.[^1] For young people aged 15 to 24 it jumped to 13.7%, and Ontario's rate rose to 7.3%.[^1] It is the third month of losses in a row; private-sector jobs fell by 53,000 while public-sector jobs rose by 50,000, and economists had expected a gain.[^2] Markets put about a 35% chance on another Bank of Canada rate rise on Dec 9, after it lifted its rate to 2.5% in October.[^2]

In Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne are touring the country to sell last week's budget, while Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre calls it a "costly credit-card budget".[^3] The House resumed debate on Friday on a Conservative amendment. The final budget vote is a test of confidence, but with a Liberal majority its outcome is "not in serious doubt", The Hub reports.[^4]

On trade, Carney welcomed plans by US Democrats, who won both houses of Congress, to roll back tariffs on Canada, but relief is not immediate: the new Congress sits in January and the president can veto bills.[^5]

For Ontario classrooms: elementary teachers (ETFO) start strike votes today, through Nov 18; Catholic teachers vote Nov 12-13, and high-school teachers and education workers are already voting.[^6] Talks are stuck over the province's push to bargain more issues centrally, and CUPE expects a labour board ruling in late November that could restart them. A "yes" vote does not mean an immediate strike.[^6]
differences: Statistics Canada calls October employment "little changed"; economists quoted by The Canadian Press are concerned because losses now reach beyond trade-hit industries.[^1][^2]
